Until a decade or two ago
column2: the centers of many Western cities were  emptying while their edges were spreading. This was not for the reasons  normally cited. Neither the car nor the motorway caused suburban sprawl
column3: although they sped it up: cities were spreading before either came along.

column1: Nor was the flight to the suburbs caused by racism. Whites fled  inner-city neighborhoods that were becoming black
column2: but they also fled ones that  were not. Planning and zoning rules encouraged sprawl
column3: as did tax breaks for  home ownership--but cities spread regardless of these. The real cause was mass  affluence. As people grew richer
column4: they demanded more privacy and space. Only a  few could afford that in city centers; the rest moved out.

column1: The same process is now occurring in the developing world
column2: but  much more quickly. The pop-ulation density of metropolitan Beijing has  collapsed since 1970
column3: falling from 425 people per hectare to 65. Indian cities  are following; Brazil's are ahead. And suburbanization has a long way to run.  Beijing is now about as crowded as metropolitan Chicago was at its most closely  packed
column4: in the 1920s. Since then Chicago's density has fallen by almost three-quarters.

column1: This is welcome. Romantic notions of sociable
column2: high-density  living--notions pushed
column3: for the most part
column4: by people who themselves occupy  rather spacious residences--ignore the squalor and lack of privacy to be found  in Kinshasa
column5: Mumbai or the other crowded cities of the poor world.

column1: Many of them are far too dense for dignified living
column2: and need to  spread out.

column1: The Western suburbs to which so many aspire are healthier than  their detractors say. The modern Stepfords are no longer white monocultures
column2: but that is progress. For every Ferguson there are many American suburbs that  have quietly become black
column3: Hispanic or Asian
column4: or a blend of every-one.  Picaresque accounts of decay overlook the fact that America's suburbs are half  as criminal and a little more than half as poor as central cities. Even as  urban centers revive
column5: more Americans move from city centre to suburb than go  the other way.

column1: But the West has also made mistakes
column2: from which the rest of the  world can learn. The first lesson is that suburban sprawl imposes costs on  everyone. Suburbanites tend to use more roads and consume more carbon than  urbanites (though perhaps not as much as distant commuters forced out by green  belts). But this damage can be alleviated by a carbon tax
column3: by toll roads and by  charging for parking. Many cities in the emerging world have followed the  foolish American practice of re-quiring property developers to provide a  certain number of parking spaces for every building--something that makes  commuting by car much more attractive than it would be otherwise. Scrap-ping  them would give public transport a chance.

column1: The second is that it is foolish to try to stop the spread of  suburbs. Green belts
column2: the most ef-fective method for doing this
column3: push up  property prices and encourage long-distance commuting. The cost of housing in  London
column5: went up by 19% in the past year
column6: reflecting not just  the city's strong economy but also the impossibility of building on its edges.  The insistence on big minimum lot sizes in some American suburbs and rural  areas has much the same effect. Cities that try to prevent growth through green  belts often end up weakening themselves

column1: A wiser policy would be to plan for huge expansion. Acquire strips  of land for roads and rail-ways
column2: and chunks for parks
column3: before the city sprawls  into them. New York's 19th-century governors decided where Central Park was  going to go long before the city reached it. New York went on to develop in a  way that they could not have imagined
column4: but the park is still there. This is not  the state control of the new-town planner--that confident soul who believes he  knows where people will want to live and work
column5: and how they will get from one  to the other. It is the realism needed to manage the inevitable. A model of  living that has broadly worked well in the West is spreading
column6: adapting to local  conditions as it goes. We should all look forward to the time when Chinese and  Indian teenagers write sulky songs about the appalling dullness of suburbia.
